item.title: Feedback: Forum Crit Team - Staff Post
item.content:encoded:
Author, per the new required reading forum guidelines: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-13282684/required-reading:how-to-use-this-forum-ideas please fill out the new concept template to seek feedback on your idea. In addition, linking to a sandbox containing a draft isn't allowed in the ideas forum unless a reviewer asks to see it.

Remember to please edit your previous post using the "edit" function under the "options" tab to the lower right of your first comment rather than creating a new thread.

Once you have revised your post accordingly, please reach out to reviewers to request that they look at your thread. You can find a list of ways to contact reviewers in this thread: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-13282692/how-to-get-more-reviews

item.title: Feedback: Forum Crit Team - Staff Post
item.content:encoded:
BUT, I’m pretty sure you’re not allowed to use the sandbox until you get greenlit.

This isn't true; users aren't allowed to post a link to their sandbox in the Drafts Critique forum without greenlights (unless they have a successful mainsite article already), but they are allowed to make and write a draft without greenlights.

In future, it's generally best to flag this kinda thing to staff (either in #site17 on IRC or via PMs) instead of dealing with it yourself.

item.title: One More Week: One More Week
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Urban Legend

Page Layout: Standard description, some interview

Elevator Pitch: SCP-XXXX is a beaten backpack with UC, Santa Cruz, patches on it. Once opened the person opening it is slowly replaced, physically and mentally, with a young philosophy student who then returns to exploring the continental United States. He also writes about his experiences, which helps pay his way.

Central Narrative: In 1989 Charles Anton Page decided to drop out of college and explore America; he felt trapped and needed to run away. He quickly adopted a "one week at a time" philosophy, where he'd find odd jobs and beg in order to obtain enough to buy a bus ticket and some food, and then would take off on the next leg of his journey.

A year or so later, he was robbed and left for dead, and would eventually succumb to his wounds. The body was never recovered. His backpack, and the contents therein, were pawned at a local pawn shop. Someone bought the backpack, and over the next few hours was transformed into a virtual clone of Page, but without the knowledge of his death or that he was leading an extended life.

He is able to live for one week (168 hours) at a time before copies of the wounds that killed him appear on his body, and he then quickly succumbs to them. Once someone finds and opens the backpack, he is yet again allowed to live for another week, but with the usual memory lapse.

While he has adapted to the modern world somewhat (he writes a blog instead of magazine articles), he is still driven to explore the continental United States. He just does it one week at a time.

Hook/Attention Grabber: A basic urban legend about a youth cut short but still trying to find a way to accomplish his dream of exploring the United States through a mix of odd jobs, bus tickets, and hitchhiking, one week at a time.

item.title: {Seeking Greenlight} The World's Best Pizza.: {Seeking Greenlight} The World's Best Pizza.
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article
Genre (Optional): Comedy, Weirdness, short and sweet

Elevator Pitch: The Foundation stumbles upon a small family-owned restaurant that happens to serve infallibly, undeniably good food.

Central Narrative: After being flagged by CHORUS, A social mapping AIC designed to detect intense spikes in mood, a small pizzeria finds itself under the attention of the Foundation. The restaurant, known as Giacomo's Pizza, makes the pretty standard claim that it serves "The World's Best." The thing is, for this bistro, that might actually be true. Anyone who tries Giacomo's pies agrees that they're the best they ever tasted -or will taste- to the point of profound satisfaction. The thing is, the foundation can't figure out why. It's just normal pizza; nothing memetic, nothing thaumaturgic, nothing chemical. In the end, when the lead researcher breaks down to the current Giacomo in charge, tearfully asking them what's so special about their pizza they merely reply "Simple. They're made with love."
Hook/Attention-Grabber: The hook of the article lies in the surrealist concept of an item of food being objectively "the best." As well as the intrigue of the eyecatching associated image:

Image block within
Close and return

Additional Notes:
While this article takes on a comedic tone, I do not intend it to be a -J. Many Skips turn funny concepts into sound articles, and I want this to be one of them.

item.title: Tale 1 of Tau-13: Tale 1 of Tau-13
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: Tale

Genre(s): Horror, Action

Page Layout: Given that this is a tale, I was going to write it like your standard narrative-driven novel. This is also the format I write most things in, save aspects of the SCP article I've drafted.

Elevator Pitch:

  • This first one will detail the team's first mission together, with flashbacks to their lives together in training.
  • The mission will involve them investigating a cult-like organization, who have been reportedly been kidnapping locals from a nearby town.
  • Upon investigation, they learn that the cult has been worshiping a horrible, Lovecraftian monster.
  • They, of course, go in for expulsion and containment.
  • They have a hard-fought battle, and through some stupid, neglectful mistakes, they lose their private to the monster.
  • Since they had all grown together in training and just as good friends, the sight of their private getting killed, combined with the psychic effects of the monstrosity, drive them very near to the edge of insanity.
  • After eventually routing out the cult, they return with broken minds. I'm thinking I'll have the Foundation use amnestics to make them forget the horrors, but deep down they still have that vastly stronger, Pavlovian-esque drive to protect each other and all innocents from these, and similar, horrors1.

Central Narrative: With the above in mind, the context is related to my SCP article currently in the Draft Critique forum. The second team that gets sent in is the team that will be written about here, and these tales will be sued to better describe their friendly relationship. This first tale in particular will describe why they are the way they are, and why they do what they do. It will describe their relationship and their drive.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: I'd like to think it's unique and interesting because I will be using it, and subsequent tales, to tie all of my in-universe work together. I don't know how original this is, but I hope to add unique spins on the way character and plot development occurs.

Additional Notes: I wouldn't mind ideas on how to improve uniqueness and originality. And please, be brutally honest. If there's something you don't like, or something you do like, I'd greatly appreciate knowing what and why. Thank you in advance!

Footnotes
1. to be used for subsequent tales involving the team.

item.title: After Hours: Re: After Hours
item.content:encoded:
I'm willing to give a greenlight for this concept. I'd like to highlight a few things that are important.

The audio logs will explore the relationship between the two members of After Hours, developing their characters and showing their love for their work. In the end, it's revealed that the anomaly is a time capsule of some sort, meant to store the greatest moments of their lives.

This will be the crux of your story. You have to convey this clearly or else this article will have trouble gaining ground with a reader. Without this, you just have a ghost nightclub, which, don't get me wrong I like, would need a different tone, probably comedic, to work. With the more emotional side here, which once again is what your article should stand on, you need to give us characters that we can connect with.

Two people's love for music and each other is detailed as a faint memory through an eternal party. The anomaly is their happy ending- getting to perform for their fans and themselves until the end of time. It's an homage to parties and the love of musical expression that takes the reader on an emotional ride.

I believe this will do a suitable job of conveying the themes you're going for. Just be sure that the memory aspect is explored along with concluding with the end of time bit.

Overall, I see this succeeding, good luck!

item.title: The Reality Dreamer: Re: The Reality Dreamer
item.content:encoded:
PM request placeholder

Alrighty then, let's take another look, shall we?

+Let's do it!
-Let's do it!

The article will have slow emotional progression disguised by the use of containment updates which contain "range updates" showing spikes and decreases with notes alongside.

Really, this is the part that impresses me most. Using a bland, emotionless scientific document to portray deeply emotional occurrences is very clever to me and the moment you stated this, I was more intrigued.

Sometime after the SCP reaches a containable situation, his wife's body dies while asleep and her mind becomes stuck with him in the dream.

I'm struggling to think of how you could portray this because this seems a little too…convenient?

Sometime after the above bullet, there is a second strong interview with him where the full extent of his progression is shown to the reader.

Hmmmmmm I have a funny idea that I'm not sure if you'll be on board with or not.

Maybe have one personnel offer their own takes on it whenever they write down a note. Or speak to their director or some such. Having a Foundation personnel get emotional from witnessing the emotional scene. It would be…weird.

We, the readers, aren't witnessing ANYTHING in the dreams. We're reading as a third perspective while the document shows personnel from a secondary perspective.

So, like, we're witnessing an empathetic researcher get emotional over an emotional scene we're not allowed to directly witness to show just how disconnected this SCP is.

You see what I'm getting at?

I feel like you could find a way to loop the researcher's observations into the Containment Procedures and Description in a way where it all clicks and makes sense in the end and makes it super emotional.

Apologies if this point in particular is a little confusing or if I'm being unclear.

Either way, you seem to have a solid grasp on what story you want to tell. You're passionate, persistent and adamant about wanting to tell this story.

So. Here's your GREENLIGHT.

I'm still kinda worried about how this will be presented in the end, but that's what critique and drafting are for.

Feel free to PM me for draft crit if you wish.

Good luck!

item.title: Monomythic Rite (working title): Re: Monomythic Rite (working title)
item.content:encoded:
In one experiment, the Foundation selects a woman to conduct the rite, only to discover the ritual was not designed for that - this log makes up most of the article. The ritual goes off track unpredictably, breaking down into incoherency, and it is solely her job to put things back on track before it's too late.

So it seems like this is the big meat of the story you're wanting to tell here and I guess what I really want to know is more about this: what happens? How does the ritual change? How does she get on with trying to get things back on track?

I'm a little unclear how this ritual actually works: it's based off the monomyth but like, how do people start it? What's the standard progression of it look like?

item.title: The magician that create more SCP.: Re: The magician that create more SCP.
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

My biggest concerns with this concept are two fold.

One: how are you going to make the creation of other SCPs interesting? My concern is that this feels like it could easily feel like a bland list of weird things which doesn't really go anywhere, particularly since the end cap to this piece is an interview explaining why the magician did this, which feels disconnected from the big list of SCPs they made.

It also feels like this is the kinda broad scope thing that can be hard to make interesting: if a SCP can produce any conceivable thing, a list of things it produced isn't very interesting? It generally needs to have some kinda theme or way to surprise a reader (e.g., if it makes things out of water, and finishes up making a person, that can work because we don't really expect it to go there).

Two: why does the magician make SCPs? It feels like the interview at the end talking about this is gonna feel super info-dumpy and I'm not sure you have enough here to make it feel interesting to read? In particular, the why of making it is only interesting if it's answer affects how we think about this.

My thoughts here are: figure out a way to do something interesting with the magician making SCPs. Like, maybe he keeps making SCPs and trying to break out and the Foundation keeps containing him and we can see him spiralling into despair as all his attempts are quashed; though this might be hard to end satisfyingly without him dying. Or perhaps the Foundation uses him to make useful stuff and he gradually begins to feel used and stuff; or whatever. Idk: at the end of the day, it feels like you'll need to do something more interesting with the concept than showing us a bunch of SCPs it made and then an interview.

item.title: Reanimation SCP - Seeking Greenlights: Re: Reanimation SCP - Seeking Greenlights
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

The Crystal is sentient, and an entity inhabits it.

This is the first the crystal is mentioned and it's not exactly clear what it's role is here: I'm assuming it's the thing that actually does the reanimation?

and it's eventually discovered he is not who he says he is.

who is he? the implication i'm getting here is that it doesn't really matter cos the focus after this switches to the crystal but?

It's a demonic entity trapped within the Crystal, reduced to a parasite, feeding off life-energy to survive.

My concern with this big reveal here is that it feels like it'd produce a reaction best described as 'okay but so what?'

I think my big concern with this is it's structured like a series of big reveals but none of the reveals feel like they have real narrative weight: the problem is that a lot of the time, the reveal doesn't really significantly change our understanding of what's happening. Like, consider the hivemind reveal: we find out it's a parasitic life form and our reaction then is 'huh that's weird' but there's not really any further implications from there? This is in part because it's entire motivation is 'trying to survive', which like, everything does; as opposed to like, trying to achieve a specific aim.

It also feels like it really needs to tap into some kinda primal fear or emotion here: like, if this was centred around the fear of being replaced or something, it'd end up feeling a lot more impactful to me. As it is, there feels like this has a real lack of emotional response here: all of this happens but it never feels like it's impactful.

item.title: "Now thats what I call existence": Re: "Now thats what I call existence"
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open
[-] Close

Here's some crit:

"transport any listener"

This is a bit unclear, how do they get back, they obviously do since there's data on the SCP, but how?

"Nothing actually dangerous happens to the researchers."

Danger is not synonymous with good storytelling, but there's just nothing for excitement at all, a kitted out research team moves down the hall to find… nothing but more cd's.

"almost every single version of humanity has had it in them to at *least* make one version."

Is this an anomalous property, that every version of Earth with humans creates this CD?

It's a fun idea, a cool infinite hall of CD's, but nothing happens there. Maybe some of the CD's are cognitohazards? That's just a spitball, but there needs to be something other than "cool room of CD's" it needs to have an associated narrative.
